entries.title: Nüwa mends the sky
entries.dateNote: Huainanzi compiled c. 139 BCE; tradition older
entries.mainstream: In Chinese mythology Nüwa is a mother goddess who moulded humans from clay. In the Huainanzi (2nd century BCE), the pillars of Heaven break, the sky collapses and floods spread, and Nüwa patches the sky with five-coloured stones and props it up with a giant turtle's legs.

alternatives.label: Sky catastrophe memory
alternatives.text: Some writers read the collapsing sky and flood as a memory of a cosmic impact or great flood (speculative).

entries.title: Bakunawa, the moon-eating serpent
entries.dateNote: Pre-colonial oral tradition; date schematic
entries.mainstream: In Philippine mythology the Bakunawa is a giant sea or sky serpent that rises to swallow the moon, causing eclipses. Its movements were used as a calendar system by babaylan priestesses. Through Indian influence it was syncretised with the Nāga and the eclipse deities Rahu and Ketu.

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural pattern
alternatives.text: Eclipse-devouring creatures also appear in Hindu (Rahu), Norse (sky wolves) and Chinese (celestial dog) traditions.

entries.title: Naga fireballs of the Mekong
entries.dateNote: Lights said to be centuries old; mass public events since c. 1990s
entries.mainstream: Glowing reddish balls are reported to rise from the Mekong River in Thailand and Laos, especially around the end of Buddhist Lent (Wan Ok Phansa) in October. Locally they are attributed to the phaya nak, a giant serpent living in the river, and the event draws large crowds.

alternatives.label: Natural gas
alternatives.text: One hypothesis is ignition of phosphine or methane from river sediments; critics say such gas would not ignite or stay lit as described.

alternatives.label: Human-made
alternatives.text: A Thai biologist analysing footage concluded the lights were flares fired from the far bank; others dispute this.

alternatives.label: Supernatural
alternatives.text: Many locals see the Naga as the true source, a religious view that cannot be tested.

entries.title: Kumari Kandam (lost Tamil continent)
entries.dateNote: Kadalkol story in an early-medieval commentary; earlier hints in Sangam verses; "Kumari Kandam" concept 20th c.
entries.mainstream: Tamil literary tradition tells of Pandyan lands "seized by the ocean" (kadalkol), including the cities of the first two Tamil Sangams. Twentieth-century Tamil revivalists merged this with the European Lemuria idea, picturing a sunken Tamil continent in the Indian Ocean called Kumari Kandam.

alternatives.label: Sea-level memory
alternatives.text: Some suggest the stories echo real coastal losses: post-glacial sea-level rise or later storms and tsunamis, such as the flood that Manimekalai says destroyed Kaverippumpattinam (speculative to partly plausible).

alternatives.label: Geology
alternatives.text: Plate tectonics rules out a sunken continent in the Indian Ocean during human times.

entries.title: 1561 celestial phenomenon over Nuremberg
entries.mainstream: A broadsheet by Hans Glaser reports that at dawn on 14 April 1561 many people in Nuremberg saw crosses, spheres, crescents and cylinders in an apparent "battle" in the sky out of the sun, followed by a large black triangular object and spheres falling to earth in smoke.

alternatives.label: Atmospheric optics
alternatives.text: Sceptics and many historians interpret it as a vivid sun-dog or halo display, described through the religious-omen conventions of the time.

alternatives.label: UFO interpretation
alternatives.text: Ufologists have proposed that observers saw extraterrestrial craft (speculative).

entries.title: 1976 Tehran UFO incident
entries.mainstream: On 19 September 1976, civilians and military personnel over Tehran saw a bright object, also tracked on radar. Two Imperial Iranian Air Force F-4 jets reported losing instruments and communications as they approached it, and one reported a temporary weapons failure. A US military report on the case was distributed to the DIA, CIA, State Department and White House.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Philip Klass and James Oberg argued the pilots initially saw a bright astronomical object (probably Jupiter) and that the failures came from equipment faults and stress.

alternatives.label: Genuine anomaly
alternatives.text: Ufologists regard it as one of the best multi-witness, radar-supported cases.

entries.title: Colares "chupa-chupa" lights and Operação Prato
entries.mainstream: In 1977 residents of Colares island (Pará, Brazil) reported lights in the sky that they said injured people, calling them "chupa-chupa". The Brazilian Air Force ran an investigation, Operação Prato (1977–78), led by Captain Uyrangê Hollanda; it closed without officially finding unusual phenomena, and its documents are now in the National Archives.

alternatives.label: Real phenomenon
alternatives.text: In a 1997 interview with ufologists, Hollanda recounted the operation's experiences; he died three months later, apparently by suicide, which drew conspiracy interest. Ufologists treat the case as significant.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Others suggest mass panic, misidentified lights and medical conditions explain the reports.

entries.title: Disappearance of Frederick Valentich
entries.mainstream: On 21 October 1978, 20-year-old pilot Frederick Valentich, flying a Cessna 182 over Bass Strait, Australia, told Melbourne air traffic control that an unknown aircraft was hovering above him and his engine was running rough, and said "it's not an aircraft". He and the plane were never found.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Investigators considered disorientation (possibly flying upside down and seeing his own lights reflected in the water) or an accident; the Department of Transport could not determine the cause and presumed the loss fatal.

alternatives.label: UFO interpretation
alternatives.text: Ufologists cite belated reports of UFO sightings that night (speculative).

entries.title: Hessdalen lights
entries.dateNote: Reports since at least 1930s; peak 1981–84
entries.mainstream: Unexplained lights have been reported in the Hessdalen valley in central Norway since at least the 1930s, with a peak of 15–20 sightings a week in 1981–84. Project Hessdalen (from 1983) and later automated stations run by Østfold University College and Italian researchers have recorded them; the phenomenon itself is real and documented, but its cause is unknown.

alternatives.label: Natural physics
alternatives.text: Proposed explanations include combustion of airborne dust (possibly linked to local scandium deposits) or a dusty plasma formed by radon decay; no consensus.

alternatives.label: Unknown intelligence
alternatives.text: Some ufologists suggest an intelligent or non-human origin (speculative).

entries.title: AARO historical UAP report (2024)
entries.mainstream: The Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), set up in 2022, published a report in March 2024 on the historical record of US government UAP investigations from 1945. It found no evidence that any sighting involved extraterrestrial technology. It also revealed a proposed, never-approved DHS programme ("Kona Blue") to reverse-engineer any craft obtained, and rejected its advocates' claims.

alternatives.label: Cover-up claims
alternatives.text: Whistle-blowers and some members of Congress maintain that crash-retrieval programmes exist and were withheld from AARO; no public evidence has confirmed this (disputed).

alternatives.label: Unresolved cases
alternatives.text: A share of reported UAP cases remain unexplained because of insufficient data, which both sides cite.

entries.title: Cardiff Giant
entries.mainstream: A 3 m "petrified man" dug up on 16 October 1869 on William Newell's farm in Cardiff, New York, which became a paid attraction. It was carved from gypsum on the orders of tobacconist George Hull, reportedly after an argument about biblical giants; P. T. Barnum even exhibited a copy.

entries.title: Japanese Paleolithic hoax (Fujimura)
entries.mainstream: From the 1970s, amateur archaeologist Shinichi Fujimura "found" ever-older Lower and Middle Palaeolithic artefacts in Japan, some sites (e.g. Zazaragi) becoming national historic sites. On 5 November 2000 the Mainichi Shimbun published hidden-camera footage of him planting artefacts; he confessed, and reviews of his sites rewrote Japan's early prehistory.
entries.changed: 1970s–90s: Fujimura sites push Japanese occupation far back into the Lower Palaeolithic. 2000: exposed. 2003: Japanese Archaeological Association review confirms the hoax.

entries.title: Coelacanth: the "extinct" fish found alive
entries.mainstream: Coelacanths were known only as fossils and thought to have died out about 66 million years ago. On 22 December 1938, museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted one in a fisherman's catch off the Chalumna River, South Africa; J. L. B. Smith described it as Latimeria. Populations were later found off the Comoros, and a second species in Indonesia (late 1990s).
entries.changed: Before 1938: extinct since the Cretaceous. 1938: living specimen. 1990s: Indonesian species.

entries.title: L'Aigle 1803: stones from the sky accepted
entries.mainstream: Before 1803 many scientists dismissed reports of stones falling from the sky as superstition, despite Ernst Chladni's 1794 argument that they came from space. On 26 April 1803 more than 3,000 fragments fell on L'Aigle, Normandy, and Jean-Baptiste Biot's investigation for the French Academy convinced scientists that meteorites are real.
entries.changed: Pre-1794: falling stones widely dismissed. 1794: Chladni. 1803: L'Aigle settles the question.

entries.title: Lemuria and Mu (lost continents)
entries.mainstream: Lemuria was proposed in 1864 by zoologist Philip Sclater as a sunken land bridge in the Indian Ocean to explain lemur distributions, and Ernst Haeckel even suggested it as humanity's homeland. Plate tectonics made it unnecessary. Occultists (Blavatsky, 1888) and writers such as Augustus Le Plongeon and James Churchward (Mu, Pacific) recast it as a lost civilisation.

alternatives.label: Esoteric tradition
alternatives.text: Theosophical and New Age groups still describe Lemuria/Mu as a spiritual ancestral homeland (belief rather than testable claim).

alternatives.label: Geology
alternatives.text: Geologists state that a continent cannot sink in the time frames claimed; ocean-floor data show no sunken continent.

entries.changed: 1864: scientific hypothesis. 1880s–1920s: occult and lost-civilisation versions. Mid-20th c.: plate tectonics retires the scientific idea.

entries.title: Vredefort impact structure
entries.mainstream: The eroded remains of one of the largest impact structures on Earth, in the Free State, South Africa, dated to about 2.023 billion years ago (±4 million). The original crater is estimated at 170–300 km across; erosion of 7–11 km has removed it, leaving the Vredefort Dome (the rebounded central uplift). It is among the oldest accepted impact structures, after Yarrabubba. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.

alternatives.label: Impactor size
alternatives.text: Older estimates put the asteroid at 10–15 km across; studies around 2022 suggest 20–25 km, which researchers say fits the shock features better.

entries.changed: 1937: Albritton and Boon propose an impact. 1961: Dietz and Hargraves find shatter cones, establishing the impact origin. 2005: UNESCO listing.

entries.title: Homo naledi and the disputed cave "burials"
entries.mainstream: A small-brained human species (brain 465–610 cm³, about 1.44 m tall) found in 2013 by cavers deep in the Rising Star Cave system, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa: more than 1,550 bone pieces from at least 15 individuals. In 2017 the remains were dated to 335,000–236,000 years ago, much younger than first expected for such a mosaic anatomy.

alternatives.label: Deliberate burial (excavators)
alternatives.text: Lee Berger, Paul Dirks and colleagues argue the bodies were deliberately carried or placed in the chamber, and in 2023 proposed burials and engraved signs; if true this would be the oldest known hominin burial.

alternatives.label: Natural deposition (critics)
alternatives.text: Other researchers (e.g. Val 2016, Egeland et al. 2018, Foecke et al. 2025) argue the evidence is insufficient and that natural processes or non-burial deposition have not been ruled out; reviewers of the 2023 papers were largely critical.

entries.changed: 2015: species named; age unknown, often assumed 1–2 million years. 2017: dated to 335,000–236,000 years. 2023–2025: burial claims published and contested.

entries.title: Madjedbebe: the oldest dated site in Australia?
entries.dateNote: Proposed c. 65,000 ± 6,000 years ago; at least 50,000 years widely accepted
entries.mainstream: A sandstone rock shelter in Arnhem Land, on Mirarr country, with more than 100,000 artefacts including ground stone axe heads, grinding stones and ground ochre. Occupation of at least 50,000 years has been widely accepted since the 1990s; excavations by Clarkson et al. (2012, 2015, published 2017) proposed about 65,000 ± 6,000 years.

alternatives.label: Younger arrival
alternatives.text: Some experts have questioned the 65,000-year estimate since its publication; the long-accepted minimum of about 50,000 years is not in dispute.

entries.changed: 1973: first test pit. 1989: thermoluminescence suggests c. 50,000 years. 2017: Clarkson et al. publish c. 65,000 years; debate continues.

sources.title: Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago

entries.title: Mungo Lady and Mungo Man
entries.dateNote: Around 40,000 years ago (estimates ranged 28,000–62,000)
entries.mainstream: Human remains found by geomorphologist Jim Bowler at the dry Lake Mungo, Willandra Lakes, New South Wales: Mungo Lady (1968), one of the world's oldest known cremations, and Mungo Man (1974), laid on his back and sprinkled with red ochre, the earliest known example of such a burial. Mungo Man is dated to around 40,000 years ago and is the oldest Homo sapiens found in Australia. Mungo Lady was repatriated to Aboriginal custodians in 1992, and both were reburied in 2022.

alternatives.label: Age debate
alternatives.text: Estimates for Mungo Man have ranged from 28,000–32,000 years (1976) to 62,000 ± 6,000 years (Thorne et al. 1999); the commonly cited age today is around 40,000 years (Bowler et al. 2003).

entries.changed: Before 1974 Aboriginal arrival in Australia was often put at c. 20,000 years ago; Mungo pushed it back to 40,000+ years.

sources.title: New ages for human occupation and climatic change at Lake Mungo, Australia

entries.title: Nabta Playa stone circle
entries.dateNote: Site used from c. 9th millennium BCE; stone circle c. 4800 BCE (Malville et al.)
entries.mainstream: Neolithic site at a former seasonal lake in the Nubian Desert of southern Egypt, used by cattle herders. Malville, Wendorf and colleagues describe a ceremonial centre (c. 6100–5600 BCE), cattle burials, a small stone circle (c. 4800 BCE) roughly aligned with summer-solstice sunrise, and megalith lines possibly aligned with bright stars (4500–3600 BCE). It is often called one of the earliest archaeoastronomical sites; a UNESCO inventory rated its solar and stellar alignments as "hypothetical".

alternatives.label: Older star-map claim (speculative)
alternatives.text: Astrophysicist Thomas Brophy proposed that stones in the circle map Orion and that alignments date to c. 6270 BCE; the original excavators replied that these dates are about 1,500 years earlier than the megalithic phase.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Some researchers note the "calendar circle" gaps are too wide for precise calendrical use and that some "aligned" stones rest on dunes and may not be in original positions.

sources.title: Megaliths and Neolithic astronomy in southern Egypt

entries.title: Kingdom of Kerma (Nubia)
entries.mainstream: Early Nubian civilisation centred at Kerma in Sudan, developing from about 2500 BCE and peaking c. 1750–1500 BCE, when it was a large urban kingdom rivalling Egypt. Remains include the huge mudbrick temple known as the Western Deffufa and royal tumuli with many human sacrifices. Egypt's New Kingdom absorbed it c. 1500 BCE; the later Kingdom of Kush may have grown out of it.

alternatives.label: Changing interpretation
alternatives.text: Excavator George Reisner (1920s) thought Kerma was an Egyptian governor's outpost; Charles Bonnet's later work showed it was an independent African kingdom, a view Egyptologists accepted only after about 20 years.

entries.changed: 1920s: Reisner sees an Egyptian trading fort. Late 20th c.: Bonnet establishes Kerma as an indigenous kingdom.

entries.title: Land of Punt ("God's Land")
entries.dateNote: Expeditions recorded c. 25th–12th centuries BCE
entries.mainstream: A trading partner known from Egyptian records from the 5th Dynasty (Sahure, 25th c. BCE) to the 20th Dynasty, supplying gold, incense, ebony, ivory and live animals. Hatshepsut's five-ship expedition is shown on her temple at Deir el-Bahri; ship remains at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis show the Red Sea port used. Egyptians sometimes called it Ta netjer, "God's Land". Its location is debated; most scholars place it in the Horn of Africa.

alternatives.label: Location from baboons
alternatives.text: Isotope studies of mummified baboons (2010, 2020) and ancient DNA (2023) point to Eritrea, Ethiopia and northwest Somalia; the 2023 DNA team suggested Adulis in Eritrea.

alternatives.label: Ancestral homeland idea
alternatives.text: Early Egyptologists such as Petrie and Budge read "God's Land" as meaning Egyptians thought Punt was their ancestral homeland; later scholars connect the name with eastern (sunrise) lands and temple goods.

alternatives.label: Arabian location
alternatives.text: Some identify Punt partly or wholly with the Arabian coast of the Red Sea.

sources.title: Mummified baboons reveal the far reach of early Egyptian mariners

media.title: How Baboons Led Us to a Lost Civilization

entries.title: Queen of Sheba, Menelik and the Ark in Aksum
entries.dateNote: Story set in Solomon's reign (traditionally 10th c. BCE); Kebra Nagast written 14th c. CE
entries.mainstream: In the Hebrew Bible an unnamed queen of Sheba brings spices, gold and gems to King Solomon (1 Kings 10). The story grew in Jewish, Ethiopian Christian and Islamic traditions (Bilqis in Arabic, Makeda in Ge'ez). Ethiopia's 14th-century Kebra Nagast makes her (as the daughter of the man who killed the serpent-king Arwe) the mother of Menelik I, ancestor of the Solomonic dynasty, who brings the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia. The Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Aksum says it holds the Ark. Historians locate Sheba (Saba) in Yemen; no trace of the queen herself has been found.

alternatives.label: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition
alternatives.text: The Ark (or the original tablets) is held in a chapel at Aksum, which only the guardian monk, appointed for life, may view; this is a matter of faith rather than a testable claim.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Edward Ullendorff said in 1992 that in 1941 he had seen the object, describing it as an empty medieval construction; the lack of access has led both Ethiopian and foreign scholars to doubt the claim.

alternatives.label: Trade-mission reading
alternatives.text: Some scholars read the visit as a memory of South Arabian incense trade with Judah; a disputed reading of the Ophel inscription has been cited in support.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion

entries.title: Ife heads and Frobenius's "African Atlantis"
entries.mainstream: Naturalistic copper-alloy heads from Ife, the sacred and royal centre of the Yoruba (Nigeria), probably made in the 14th–15th centuries, likely representing kings (Ooni). Eighteen were found in 1938 at the Wunmonije Compound; one is in the British Museum. Their realism challenged dismissive Western views of African art.

alternatives.label: Atlantis claim (debunked)
alternatives.text: After finding an earlier Ife head, German ethnologist Leo Frobenius proposed they were made by an ancient Greek colony and that Yoruba culture preserved the lost civilisation of Atlantis (press headlines in 1911). Archaeology shows they are Yoruba works.

alternatives.label: Frobenius in context
alternatives.text: Frobenius rejected the colonial idea that a "white" civilisation underlay African achievements, and W. E. B. Du Bois cited him; his Atlantis theory still assumed an outside origin.

entries.changed: 1910–1911: Frobenius links Ife to Atlantis. 1938: Wunmonije heads found; now recognised as Yoruba masterpieces of the 14th–15th c.

entries.title: Epic of Sundiata (founding of Mali)
entries.mainstream: Mande epic, kept by griots (jeliw) for centuries, about Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire (ruled c. 1235–1255). A prophecy foretells his birth; he cannot walk as a child, rises with a staff, goes into exile and returns to defeat the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235). Mansa Musa was his great-nephew. The best-known version, from griot Djeli Mamoudou Kouyaté, was published by D. T. Niane in 1960.

alternatives.label: Historical core
alternatives.text: Historians accept Sundiata as the real founder of Mali and Kirina (c. 1235) as a real battle; Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun, who travelled to Mali in the following century, provide independent information. The magical episodes are epic tradition.

alternatives.label: Oral history
alternatives.text: The epic is studied as an example of oral tradition carrying political history (and the Kouroukan Fouga "constitution") across many generations; versions differ in details.

entries.title: Mali's lost Atlantic fleet
entries.dateNote: Before Musa's accession (c. 1312); story told in Cairo in 1324
entries.mainstream: In Cairo in 1324, Mansa Musa said that his predecessor sent 200 ships (plus 200 supply ships) to find the far edge of the Atlantic; one returned, reporting a "river" in the sea (probably the Canary Current). The ruler then sailed with 2,000 ships and never came back. The only account is al-Umari's record. The ruler is popularly called "Abu Bakr II", but that name comes from a 19th-century mistranslation; Ibn Khaldun names Musa's predecessor as Muhammad ibn Qu.

alternatives.label: Reached the Americas (speculative)
alternatives.text: Ivan van Sertima and Gaoussou Diawara proposed the fleet reached the New World, citing reports in Columbus-era sources.

alternatives.label: Mainstream view
alternatives.text: Scholars note that no genuine African artefact has been found in a controlled excavation in the Americas and that there is no accepted evidence of pre-Columbian African contact.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atlantic voyage of the predecessor of Mansa Musa

entries.title: Jiahu symbols
entries.dateNote: Seventh millennium BCE (often rounded to c. 6000 BCE)
entries.mainstream: Signs incised on tortoise shells and bones at Jiahu, a Neolithic Peiligang-culture site in Henan, China (excavated 1989). Of 17 groups first identified, 11 are definite incised signs. A few resemble much later oracle-bone characters such as "eye" and "sun".

alternatives.label: Earliest writing?
alternatives.text: Some researchers see a very early writing system, partly because the tortoise shells hint at later Shang divination practice.

alternatives.label: Proto-writing / sign use
alternatives.text: A 2003 Antiquity report interpreted them not as writing but as part of a long period of sign-use that eventually led to writing; most scholars doubt they are systematic writing.

entries.title: Oracle bones: "dragon bones" that proved the Shang
entries.mainstream: Ox shoulder blades and turtle shells used for divination in the late Shang dynasty (c. 1250–1050 BCE): questions were carved, heat cracked the bone and the answer was read. About 13,000 bones with 130,000+ inscriptions are known. In the 19th century villagers near Anyang sold them as "dragon bones" for traditional medicine; in 1899 Wang Yirong recognised the marks as ancient Chinese writing. Excavations (1928–37) at Yinxu proved the Shang dynasty and its last capital were real.

alternatives.label: Lost to medicine
alternatives.text: Historian Xu Yahui notes no one knows how many inscribed bones were ground up by pharmacies before 1899.

alternatives.label: Malaria tale
alternatives.text: The story that Wang noticed the writing on his own malaria medicine is described as a legend; how he actually obtained the bones is not known.

entries.changed: Before 1899: Shang known only from later texts and sometimes doubted. 1899: inscriptions recognised. 1908: source traced to Anyang. 1928–37: excavations confirm the Shang capital.

entries.title: Plain of Jars and the giants' rice wine
entries.dateNote: Jars placed c. 1240–660 BCE (OSL); Site 1 burials 8th–13th c. CE
entries.mainstream: Thousands of large stone jars in clusters across the Xiangkhoang Plateau, Laos. Madeleine Colani (1930s) linked them to burial, and later excavations found cremated and secondary burials, beads and grave goods. Luminescence dating suggests jars were placed as early as 1240–660 BCE, while burials at Site 1 date to the 8th–13th centuries CE. The area was heavily bombed by the US Air Force during the Secret War in Laos (1960s), and only some sites have been cleared of unexploded bombs. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Local legend
alternatives.text: Lao legend tells of a race of giants whose king Khun Cheung defeated the enemy king Chao Angka and made the jars to brew and store rice wine (lau hai) for the victory feast.

alternatives.label: "Distilling vessel" idea
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggested bodies were first placed in jars to decompose before cremation and secondary burial, as in later royal funeral customs of the region.

sources.title: Excavating among the megaliths: recent research at the ‘Plain of Jars’ site 1 in Laos
Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang – Plain of Jars (UNESCO)

entries.title: The lost grave of Genghis Khan
entries.dateNote: Death August 1227; location of grave unknown
entries.mainstream: Genghis Khan died in August 1227; his grave has never been found. It is generally thought to be near the sacred mountain Burkhan Khaldun in the Khentii Mountains of Mongolia, and searches (recently with drones) face cultural objections because of the mountain's sanctity. The Genghis Khan Mausoleum in Inner Mongolia is a memorial, not his grave.

alternatives.label: Legend: no witnesses
alternatives.text: A frequently retold story says the funeral slaves were killed by guards who were themselves killed; this does not appear in contemporary sources.

alternatives.label: Legend: hidden by nature
alternatives.text: Other tales say a river was diverted over the grave (echoing stories told of Gilgamesh and Alaric), horses trampled it flat, or trees were planted over it.

alternatives.label: Legend: the weeping camel
alternatives.text: One tale says a baby camel was buried with the Khan so its mother could later lead the family back to the grave.

entries.title: Xu Fu's voyage for the elixir of life
entries.mainstream: Xu Fu, a court sorcerer of Qin Shi Huang, was sent twice (219–210 BCE) to find the elixir of immortality on the mythical Mount Penglai in the eastern sea, reportedly with thousands of young men and women. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian says he reached a land of "flat plains and wide swamps", made himself king and never returned.

alternatives.label: Legend in Japan
alternatives.text: From a 10th-century account by the monk Yichu onward, Xu Fu is said to have landed in Japan; many Japanese shrines honour him as a bringer of farming, medicine and silk. Some writers even identified him with Emperor Jimmu (speculative).

alternatives.label: Mainstream view
alternatives.text: The Japanese landing first appears in a text written more than 1,100 years after the voyage, and the accounts crediting him with new crops and techniques are also much later.

entries.title: Tambora 1815: the lost kingdom and the year without a summer
entries.mainstream: The April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia (VEI 7) is the most powerful in recorded history. Pyroclastic flows destroyed the village and kingdom of Tambora; deaths from the eruption, famine and disease are estimated at roughly 71,000–100,000. The ash veil helped cause the "Year Without a Summer" in 1816, with harvest failures in many parts of the world. In 2004 excavations found a house and its inhabitants buried under ash, prompting the label "Pompeii of the East".

alternatives.label: Lost language
alternatives.text: The Tambora language, wiped out by the eruption, appears to have been an isolate, possibly the last survivor of the pre-Austronesian languages of central Indonesia.

entries.title: Kuk Swamp: farming invented in New Guinea
entries.dateNote: Earliest drainage c. 9,000 years ago (c. 7000 BCE)
entries.mainstream: Wetland site in the Wahgi Valley highlands of Papua New Guinea with drainage ditches and planting features from about 9,000 years ago, used to grow taro, with bananas and sugar cane cultivated from about 6,900–6,400 years ago. UNESCO (2008) lists it as one of the few places where people independently invented agriculture.

sources.title: Origins of Agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the Highlands of New Guinea

entries.title: Kuwae: the island swallowed by an eruption
entries.dateNote: 15th century CE; once dated 1452 from ice cores, now uncertain
entries.mainstream: Oral traditions of Tongoa, Vanuatu, tell of a land called Kuwae destroyed by a great eruption; in the legend of Ti Tongoa Liseiriki a young man escapes along the coast to Tongariki. Thick 15th-century pyroclastic deposits blanket Tongoa and Epi, and a 6 × 12 km submarine caldera between them was found in 1994 and named Kuwae caldera.

alternatives.label: Huge eruption linked to ice cores
alternatives.text: Earlier studies linked Kuwae to a large sulphate spike in Antarctic ice dated 1452–1453 and estimated 30–60 km³ of magma; a 2012 study re-dated the spike to 1458, and tephra geochemistry does not match Kuwae, so the source remains unidentified.

alternatives.label: Smaller eruption
alternatives.text: Another team argues the deposits indicate only a small to moderate eruption, possibly from a different caldera south of Tongoa, where the traditions actually place Kuwae.

sources.title: The Kuwae (Vanuatu) eruption of AD 1452: potential magnitude and volatile release

entries.title: Haast's eagle and the pouākai legend
entries.dateNote: Coexisted with Māori from c. 1250–1275 until extinction c. 1445
entries.mainstream: The largest eagle known (10–18 kg), Hieraaetus moorei lived on New Zealand's South Island and hunted moa weighing up to 200 kg. Ancient DNA (2005) showed its closest relatives are small Hieraaetus eagles, implying very rapid growth in size. After Māori arrived (c. 1250–1275) the moa were hunted out, and the eagle died out about 1445. Māori rock art in South Canterbury appears to depict it.

alternatives.label: Pouākai / Hōkioi legends
alternatives.text: The eagle is commonly accepted as the pouākai of Māori tradition, a giant bird said to kill people as well as moa, which scientists consider physically plausible.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Some argue the hakawai and hōkioi stories refer instead to a snipe, and that pouākai may not refer to Haast's eagle since it is not known from the North Island.

sources.title: Ancient DNA Provides New Insights into the Evolutionary History of New Zealand's Extinct Giant Eagle

entries.title: Great Serpent Mound
entries.dateNote: c. 300 BCE (Adena) or c. 1070 CE (Fort Ancient), dates debated
entries.mainstream: A 411 m (1,348 ft) long effigy mound in Adams County, Ohio, the largest serpent effigy known, with a triple-coiled tail and an open mouth around an oval feature. First surveyed by Squier and Davis (1848). It sits on the Serpent Mound crater, a 14 km impact structure formed 252–330 million years ago. Who built it, and when, is debated.

alternatives.label: Adena builders, c. 300 BCE
alternatives.text: Radiocarbon studies from 2014 onward (e.g. Romain et al. 2017), corroborated in 2019, place construction c. 300 BCE by Adena people, with repair or rebuilding c. 1100 CE.

alternatives.label: Fort Ancient builders, c. 1070 CE
alternatives.text: Charcoal from a reopened trench (1996) gave c. 1070 CE; Brad Lepper argues the dated "organic sediment" from cores can read too old, and that serpent imagery and effigy mounds fit the Fort Ancient culture. Some suggest Halley's Comet (1066) inspired it (speculative).

alternatives.label: Religious / New Age readings
alternatives.text: In 1901 Rev. Landon West claimed it marked the Garden of Eden; today New Age visitors and others see astronomical or spiritual meanings (belief rather than testable claim).

sources.title: Radiocarbon Dates Reveal Serpent Mound Is More than Two Thousand Years Old

entries.title: The "lost race" of the Mound Builders
entries.mainstream: Indigenous peoples of eastern North America built earthen mounds for over 5,000 years, from Watson Brake (c. 3500 BCE) to Mississippian centres such as Cahokia. In the 19th century many Americans claimed instead that a vanished "lost race" built them: Israelites, Vikings, Welsh, people from Atlantis, or giants. Newspapers reported giant skeletons, and Josiah Priest's American Antiquities (1833) popularised the idea. Cyrus Thomas's 1894 Bureau of Ethnology report established that ancestors of Native Americans built the mounds.

alternatives.label: Why it spread
alternatives.text: Writers such as Robert Silverberg and Jason Colavito link the myth to racist views of Native Americans common at the time; Thomas Jefferson had already noted similarities between mound burials and Native practice.

alternatives.label: Hoaxes involved
alternatives.text: Rafinesque's Walam Olum (1836) was later argued to be a hoax, and William Pidgeon's claims were exposed as fraudulent in 1886.

alternatives.label: Modern echoes
alternatives.text: Versions linking mounds to Atlantis or Mu still circulate online (speculative).

entries.changed: 1830s–1880s: "lost race" theories popular. 1886: Pidgeon's claims exposed. 1894: Cyrus Thomas report credits Native Americans.

entries.title: Lost cities of the Amazon: from Fawcett's "Z" to lidar
entries.mainstream: Lidar surveys have mapped extensive pre-Columbian settlements in the Amazon rainforest: the Upano Valley sites in Ecuador (from c. 500 BCE, over a millennium earlier than other known complex Amazonian societies; about 6,000 platforms linked by roads, Science 2024) and the Casarabe culture of the Bolivian Llanos de Moxos (c. 500–1400 CE; platform mounds, pyramids up to 22 m, causeways and canals, Nature 2022).

alternatives.label: Fawcett's "Z"
alternatives.text: Explorer Percy Fawcett believed a lost city he called "Z" lay in the Mato Grosso and vanished searching for it in 1925; journalist David Grann reported (2005) that archaeologist Michael Heckenberger's work suggests a monumental culture, Kuhikugu, may have existed near where Fawcett was searching.

entries.changed: 1914: Fawcett formulates "Z". 1925: he disappears. 2015: Ecuador funds Upano lidar. 2022: Casarabe lidar published. 2024: Upano Valley lidar published.

entries.title: Classic Maya collapse
entries.dateNote: Decline mainly 8th–9th c. CE; northern cities flourished afterwards
entries.mainstream: In the 8th–9th centuries CE many southern lowland Maya cities, including Tikal, Copán, Palenque and Calakmul, stopped raising dated monuments and were abandoned. Maya civilisation continued in northern Yucatán (Chichén Itzá, Mayapán) and the highlands until the Spanish conquest (Nojpetén, 1697); millions of Maya live there today. More than 80 explanations have been proposed.

alternatives.label: Drought
alternatives.text: Lake sediments and cave records show severe drought; Evans et al. (2018) estimated annual rainfall fell 41–54%, up to 70% at peak. Drought is now the leading single explanation.

alternatives.label: Rupture, not collapse
alternatives.text: Many scholars prefer "rupture" or transformation, pointing to warfare, political change (abandonment of the ajawlel system of kingship) and reduced trade as well as climate.

entries.title: Omens of the conquest: was Cortés taken for Quetzalcoatl?
entries.dateNote: Omens said to begin c. 1509–1517; Spanish arrival 1519
entries.mainstream: Nahua accounts written after the fall of Tenochtitlan (1521) describe eight omens before the Spanish arrived: a column of fire in the night sky (1517), temples burning, comets in threes, a lake boiling, a weeping woman, and a bird with a mirror in its crown. A famous later story says Moctezuma believed Cortés was the god Quetzalcoatl returning in the year Ce Acatl (1519).

alternatives.label: Belief was real
alternatives.text: Historian Hugh Thomas and others describe Moctezuma as weighing whether Cortés was a god or an envoy, and some scholars think some of the omens were real events later linked to the conquest.

alternatives.label: Post-conquest invention
alternatives.text: Others note that Cortés never claimed in his letters to have been taken for a god, that the idea appears in European writings only in the 1540s, and that Spanish and friar-supervised sources had reasons to present the conquest as foretold.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

entries.title: Tokoloshe
entries.dateNote: Undated oral tradition; placed at c. 1900 for display only
entries.mainstream: In Nguni (Zulu, Xhosa and related) folklore of southern Africa the tokoloshe is a small, dwarf-like, mischievous or evil water spirit that can turn invisible by drinking water or swallowing a stone, and can be sent by a malevolent person to cause illness or death. A common protection is raising the bed on bricks; traditional healers (sangomas) or pastors may be called to banish it. It also features widely in South African satire and pop culture.

alternatives.label: Proposed natural explanation
alternatives.text: One explanation offered is that people sleeping on the floor around indoor fires in rondavels died of carbon-monoxide build-up near the ground, while those on raised beds survived, giving rise to the bed-on-bricks custom (interpretive, untested).

entries.title: Mami Wata, the African water spirit
entries.dateNote: Iconography from 15th c. contact onward; snake-charmer image 19th c.
entries.mainstream: Mami Wata ("Mother Water") is a mermaid-like water spirit or goddess of wealth, fertility, healing and beauty venerated across West, Central, East and Southern Africa and the Atlantic diaspora. Scholars trace her image to encounters with Europeans from the 15th century and European mermaid figures; from the mid-19th century a European print of the snake charmer Nala Damajanti reshaped her iconography, and Hindu imagery added a male consort, Papi Wata.

alternatives.label: Diaspora relatives
alternatives.text: Some scholars relate her to similar water spirits in the Caribbean and Latin America.

alternatives.label: Demonised
alternatives.text: Some African Christian and Islamic communities regard her as a demon.

entries.title: Rama Setu / Adam's Bridge
entries.dateNote: Ramayana composed c. 8th c. BCE–3rd c. CE; placed at 500 BCE
entries.mainstream: A 48 km chain of limestone shoals between India and Sri Lanka. In the Ramayana (composed between the 8th c. BCE and 3rd c. CE) Rama's army builds a bridge to Lanka to rescue Sita; Islamic tradition says Adam crossed it after leaving Eden (name recorded c. 1030). Geologists say the strait was dry land during the last glacial period, flooded by around 7,000 years ago, and the shoals re-emerged as sea levels fell from about 5,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Built by humans?
alternatives.text: A former Geological Survey of India director, a 2008 court submission and an episode of the Science Channel series What on Earth? claimed the structure is man-made; geologists describe the shoals as natural limestone formations.

alternatives.label: NASA images misread
alternatives.text: During protests against the Sethusamudram canal project, NASA said its satellite photos had been misinterpreted: "remote sensing images ... cannot determine whether humans were involved."

alternatives.label: Location of Lanka
alternatives.text: Many scholars place the epic's Lanka in central India rather than Sri Lanka.

entries.title: Yonaguni "underwater pyramid"
entries.mainstream: Stepped rock terraces off Yonaguni, Japan's southernmost island, found by a diver in 1986. Geologists including Robert Schoch, Wolf Wichmann, Patrick Nunn and Ogata et al. (2019) conclude they are natural Miocene sandstone (about 20 million years old) split along bedding planes and vertical joints, like similar terraces on shore. Japan's cultural agencies do not treat it as an archaeological site.

alternatives.label: Man-made monument (speculative)
alternatives.text: Marine geologist Masaaki Kimura argues it is a carved stepped monument with roads and a "stadium", first dating it to at least 10,000 years ago (possibly linked to Mu) and later (2007) to 2,000–3,000 years ago; Graham Hancock says so many odd features in one place is unlikely to be natural.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Critics note the steps are attached to bedrock, the "carvings" look like natural scratches, and strong currents explain the lack of loose blocks.

media.title: The truth behind Japan's mysterious 'Atlantis' – BBC REEL

entries.title: Sunken Dwarka and the Gulf of Khambhat "city"
entries.dateNote: Rao's date c. 1500 BCE; epic dating uncertain
entries.mainstream: In the Mahabharata's Mausala Parva, Arjuna watches the sea flood and submerge Krishna's city of Dvaraka; the Harivamsa says it was built on land "released by the ocean". Underwater surveys off modern Dwarka and Bet Dwarka (1983–1990) found walls, a stone jetty and stone anchors; the Archaeological Survey of India interprets them as a port of the Middle kingdoms period destroyed probably by coastal erosion.

alternatives.label: Dvaraka found
alternatives.text: Marine archaeologist S. R. Rao concluded the remains show a city-state of c. 1500 BCE that is reasonably the Dvaraka of the epic (based on one carbon date).

alternatives.label: Gulf of Khambhat (disputed)
alternatives.text: In 2001 India's science minister announced a submerged city in the Gulf of Khambhat older than the Indus civilisation; a dredged piece of wood dated to about 9,500 years. Archaeologists reject the dating because artefacts were dredged, not excavated, and some "tools" may be natural geofacts.

entries.title: Crystal skulls
entries.mainstream: Quartz skulls sold as Aztec or Maya relics. None comes from a documented excavation. Studies at the British Museum (1967, 1996, 2004) and a British Museum–Smithsonian study (2008) found tool marks from rotary wheels and hard abrasives, showing 19th-century or later manufacture, probably in workshops at Idar-Oberstein, Germany. Many passed through the Paris dealer Eugène Boban (from 1870). The Mitchell-Hedges "Skull of Doom", said to have been found at Lubaantun, was bought at Sotheby's in 1943.

alternatives.label: Mystical skulls (New Age)
alternatives.text: Some New Age groups claim the skulls have paranormal powers; legends of magical crystal skulls do not appear in genuine Mesoamerican traditions.

entries.changed: 1880s–1930s: skulls displayed as pre-Columbian. 1967–2008: museum studies show modern tool marks.

entries.title: The 2012 "Maya apocalypse"
entries.mainstream: 21 December 2012 ended a b'ak'tun, a 5,126-year cycle in the Mesoamerican Long Count calendar. Claims spread that the date would bring the end of the world (a collision with "Nibiru", a galactic alignment, solar storms) or a spiritual transformation. Maya scholars said no Classic Maya text predicts doom, and astronomers called the scenarios pseudoscience. The date passed with festivities at Chichén Itzá and Tikal.

alternatives.label: Spiritual-transformation reading
alternatives.text: New Age writers saw the date as the start of a new era of consciousness (belief rather than testable claim).

media.title: ScienceCasts: Why the World Didn't End Yesterday

entries.title: "Alien" Nazca mummies at Mexico's Congress
entries.mainstream: In 2017 small three-fingered "mummies" said to come from near the Nazca Lines in Peru were promoted online, and Mexican journalist Jaime Maussan presented two to a Mexican Congress hearing on UFOs on 12 September 2023, claiming a third of their DNA was of "unknown origin". UNAM said it had made no such finding. Peru's prosecutor's office (2017) and forensic archaeologist Flavio Estrada concluded they are recently made dolls of human and animal bones joined with synthetic glue and paper.

alternatives.label: Non-human beings (claim)
alternatives.text: Maussan and doctors at a second hearing (November 2023) said the bodies were once living organisms and "potential evidence of non-human life forms", while declining to certify them as extraterrestrial.

entries.changed: 2017: first videos; Peru prosecutor finds dolls. 2023: shown at Mexican Congress; experts reaffirm hoax.

entries.title: Utsuro-bune: the "hollow ship" of 1803
entries.dateNote: Event dated 22 Feb 1803 in texts written 1815–1844
entries.mainstream: Four Japanese texts (1815–1844) say that on 22 February 1803 fishermen in Hitachi Province found a round vessel like an incense burner, with windows and strange writing inside, carrying a pale young woman with red hair who spoke an unknown language and clutched a box; they set her adrift again. Folklorists such as Yanagita Kunio see it as part of a long Japanese tradition of drifting-boat tales (e.g. Princess Wake, Konjiki-hime).

alternatives.label: UFO encounter (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some ufologists cite the story as an early close encounter with an extraterrestrial craft.

alternatives.label: Foreign castaway
alternatives.text: In 1844 writer Kyokutei Bakin suggested from a book on Russian customs that the woman may have been Russian; a villager in one version suggests an exiled foreign princess.

entries.title: Varginha "ET" incident (Brazil, 1996)
entries.mainstream: On 20 January 1996 three young women in Varginha, Minas Gerais, said they saw a large-headed creature with red eyes and three bumps on its head. Rumours followed of UFOs, alien captures by the army, a hospital examination, a police officer's death and unexplained zoo animal deaths, and the case drew huge media coverage. A 1997 Brazilian military inquiry concluded the women had seen a local man nicknamed "Mudinho", crouching and dirty after heavy rain, and that military movements were routine.

alternatives.label: Captured alien (claim)
alternatives.text: Ufologists allege that one or more extraterrestrials were captured and moved by the military and that officials covered it up.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Sceptic Brian Dunning calls it a case where "literally nothing at all happened that was remotely unusual", with rumours linked together afterwards.

entries.title: Kaikōura lights (New Zealand, 1978)
entries.mainstream: On 21 December 1978 Safe Air cargo pilots saw strange lights near the Kaikōura ranges, also tracked by Wellington radar. On 30–31 December an Australian TV crew aboard another flight filmed bright lights, including a large orb that seemed to pace the aircraft; the footage was shown worldwide.

alternatives.label: Unexplained (Maccabee)
alternatives.text: US optical physicist Bruce Maccabee calculated the object was very bright and 20 m or more across, and concluded it was an unknown phenomenon.

alternatives.label: Squid boats and optics
alternatives.text: New Zealand's DSIR said the lights were most likely squid-fishing boats' lamps, with atmospheric bending of radar and light, and distortion from filming through the window; astronomers suggested Jupiter or Mars (which would not show on radar), ball lightning or meteors, and Patrick Moore reflections, a balloon or an aircraft.

entries.title: Okapi: the "African unicorn" confirmed
entries.mainstream: Europeans heard reports of an unknown forest animal, nicknamed the "African unicorn"; Henry Morton Stanley (1887) mentioned a donkey-like animal the local people called the atti. Harry Johnston, told about the animal by Congo forest people he had rescued from a showman, obtained striped skin and a skull, and the species was formally described in 1901 (first as Equus johnstoni, then Okapia johnstoni). It turned out to be a forest relative of the giraffe, found only in the northeast of the DR Congo.
entries.changed: 1887: Stanley reports the atti. 1901: described by science from skin and skull.

entries.title: The kraken and the giant squid
entries.mainstream: The kraken, a Norwegian sea monster big as an island, appears in a 1646 glossary and was described by Bishop Pontoppidan (1753). Giant squid tales are old among mariners, and zoologist Japetus Steenstrup named the giant squid Architeuthis in 1857; a French warship secured part of one in 1861. Its feeding tentacles can reach about 10 m. The first photos of a live giant squid in the wild were taken on 30 September 2004 by Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori; video followed in 2012.

alternatives.label: Legend from squid?
alternatives.text: Many think kraken stories (and perhaps the "sea monk" of c. 1550, the Caribbean Lusca or Greek Scylla) came from sightings of giant squid; claims of 20 m+ specimens remain undocumented.

entries.changed: 1753: kraken described as fact by Pontoppidan. 1857: Architeuthis named. 2004: first photos alive. 2012: first video.

entries.title: Lebombo bone: a 43,000-year-old tally?
entries.dateNote: About 42,000–43,000 years old (24 radiocarbon dates)
entries.mainstream: A baboon fibula about 8 cm long with incised notches, found in Border Cave in the Lebombo Mountains between South Africa and Eswatini. Twenty-four radiocarbon dates put it at about 42,000–43,000 years old, far older than the Ishango bone it is often confused with. A 2012 reanalysis of Border Cave organic artefacts (d'Errico et al.) concluded that its Early Later Stone Age inhabitants used notched bones "for notational purposes", alongside tools closely resembling those of later San hunter-gatherers.

alternatives.label: Tally or calendar (interpretation)
alternatives.text: The bone has been conjectured to be a tally stick; popular accounts sometimes call it a lunar calendar or the oldest mathematical object, which goes beyond what the notches alone can show.

alternatives.label: Ritual marks
alternatives.text: Its discoverer, Peter Beaumont, saw the changes in notch section (made with different cutting edges) as evidence that the marks were made during participation in rituals, like other notched objects worldwide. Even older notched bones (c. 80,000 years) exist, but it is unclear whether such notches are decorative or functional.

sources.title: Early evidence of San material culture represented by organic artifacts from Border Cave, South Africa

entries.title: The Green Sahara (African Humid Period)
entries.dateNote: c. 14,600 to c. 5,000 years ago, with interruptions
entries.mainstream: From about 14,600–14,500 years ago until roughly 6,000–5,000 years ago much of the Sahara was covered by grasses, trees and lakes, caused by changes in Earth's axial tilt, a strengthened African monsoon, vegetation and dust feedbacks and greenhouse gases. Lake Chad expanded, Lake Victoria refilled and the "Wild Nile" produced its largest recorded floods. People settled the desert, herded cattle, goats and sheep, and left rock art of swimmers and savanna animals in places that are now hyper-arid. Dry spells interrupted it during the Younger Dryas and the 8.2-kiloyear event; when it ended, people moved toward the Nile Valley and Mesopotamia, where early complex societies arose.

alternatives.label: Abrupt end
alternatives.text: deMenocal et al. (2000), using marine sediment off West Africa, argued that the humid period began and ended abruptly, within decades to centuries.

alternatives.label: Gradual end
alternatives.text: Kröpelin et al. (2008), using a lake record from northern Chad, argued for a gradual drying over thousands of years; the end may have come in several steps, including around the 4.2-kiloyear event.

alternatives.label: Link to Egypt and myth (interpretation)
alternatives.text: Researchers connect the drying with the rise of Ancient Egyptian civilisation; some also suggest that former lakes such as Nabta Playa may relate to later Egyptian religion. Alternative writers sometimes cite the wetter Sahara in support of an older Sphinx (see Sphinx water-erosion hypothesis), which mainstream Egyptology does not accept.

entries.changed: 1850: Heinrich Barth suggests past wetter climates from Saharan petroglyphs. 1920s–30s: rock art of swimmers and savanna animals strengthens the idea. Late 20th century: lake cores and marine sediments confirm and date the humid period.

entries.title: Tassili n'Ajjer and the "Round Head" paintings
entries.dateNote: Round Head period c. 7550–5050 BCE (style-based dating)
entries.mainstream: The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in the Algerian Sahara holds one of the world's great concentrations of rock art (UNESCO World Heritage Site). It is usually divided into Archaic (10,000–7500 BCE), Round Head (7550–5050 BCE), Bovidian/Pastoral, Horse and Camel periods. The Round Head paintings, by hunter-gatherers living in a green Sahara, include some of Africa's oldest and largest rock paintings (one figure over five metres tall) and show floating humanoid figures with round, featureless heads. Henri Lhote's 1950s expeditions made the art famous, but his team was later accused of faking images and of damaging paintings while brightening them for tracing and photography, reducing the original colours beyond repair.

alternatives.label: Mushroom-ritual hypothesis (speculative)
alternatives.text: Giorgio Samorini (1989) proposed that fungoid figures, such as masked dancers holding mushroom-like objects and the "mushroom shaman" of Matalem-Amazar, show ritual use of psychedelic mushrooms; Terence McKenna built on this in Food of the Gods (1992). Other researchers do not accept that the images depict mushrooms.

alternatives.label: Ritual sanctuaries
alternatives.text: Lhote regarded the painted shelters as secret sanctuaries; the concentration of Round Head motifs at particular sites is taken by researchers to suggest centres of ritual and ceremony.

entries.title: Lydenburg Heads
entries.mainstream: Seven hollow terracotta heads from Lydenburg, Mpumalanga, South Africa, among the oldest known Iron Age artworks south of the equator. Charcoal found with them dates to about 1,410 years ago (about 500 CE). Six have human features and one an animal-like snout; the two largest, big enough to be worn over a child's head, carry small figurines (perceived as lions). They may once have been covered in white slip and glittering specularite. A boy, Karl-Ludwig von Bezing, first found fragments while playing on his father's farm and later collected more in 1962 and 1966; they were reconstructed at the University of Cape Town.

alternatives.label: Use
alternatives.text: They may have been worn as masks or headdresses (small perforations suggest attachment to a framework) or were part of a significant structure; their exact purpose is unknown.

entries.title: Igbo-Ukwu bronzes
entries.dateNote: Radiocarbon c. 850 CE (9th century)
entries.mainstream: Bronze and copper objects of great intricacy from three sites at Igbo-Ukwu, Anambra State, Nigeria: Igbo Isaiah (a shrine, found in 1938 by villager Isaiah Anozie while digging beside his home), Igbo Richard (a burial chamber with a body in apparent regalia) and Igbo Jonah (a cache), excavated by Thurstan Shaw from 1959. Radiocarbon dates of about the 9th century CE made them the earliest known bronze casting in the region, centuries before other known bronzes there. Igbo-Ukwu was associated with the Kingdom of Nri, and more than 165,000 glass and carnelian beads point to long-distance trade reaching Egypt and North Africa.

alternatives.label: Outside origin (early speculation)
alternatives.text: The technical skill and lack of known prototypes led to early academic speculation that the bronzes must post-date European contact, and "phantom voyagers" were postulated as their makers.

alternatives.label: Local origin (current view)
alternatives.text: Isotope analysis shows the metals are of local origin, and radiocarbon dating confirmed a 9th-century date; a later AMS date on a textile from Igbo Isaiah (1027–1180 CE) suggests some material may be younger.

entries.title: Sungbo's Eredo and the Queen of Sheba
entries.dateNote: Disputed: 10th–11th century CE (Darling) or late 14th–15th century CE
entries.mainstream: A system of ditches and banks more than 160 km long ringing the old Ijebu kingdom near Ijebu Ode, Ogun State, Nigeria; in places the height from ditch bottom to bank top reaches 20 m. Archaeologist Patrick Darling (1999) called it the largest single monument in Africa. Its dating is disputed: some carbon dates go back to 2000 BCE (which need not date the ditch), Darling proposed the 10th–11th centuries CE, and more recent excavations point to the late 14th–early 15th century. It probably served defence and the unification of diverse communities, like similar earthworks around Ife, Ilesa and Benin. LiDAR mapping began in 2024.

alternatives.label: Bilikisu Sungbo
alternatives.text: Ijebu tradition links the Eredo to a wealthy, childless widow, Oloye Bilikisu Sungbo, who built it as her memorial; her grave is believed to be at Oke-Eiri, where Christians and Muslims make an annual pilgrimage.

alternatives.label: Queen of Sheba
alternatives.text: Some identify Bilikisu with the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis in Islamic tradition). Darling said the idea "cannot be discounted" because local people believe it, but that "the most cogent argument against it at the moment is the dating".

entries.title: "Adam's Calendar" and the Bokoni stone ruins
entries.mainstream: Thousands of stone-walled homesteads, cattle paths and agricultural terraces stretch for about 150 km along the Mpumalanga escarpment, South Africa. Archaeologists attribute them to Bokoni, an agro-pastoral society of about 1500–1820 CE that traded farm produce widely and was disrupted during the Mfecane; radiocarbon dates also showed the Lydenburg Bokoni sites predate the Pedi, overturning an older attribution. One stone circle complex, the Blaauboschkraal ruins near Emgwenya (a provincial heritage site), is popularly called "Adam's Calendar". Many sites are on private land and threatened by stone removal and vandalism.

alternatives.label: Ancient or alien builders (speculative)
alternatives.text: Michael Tellinger, influenced by Zecharia Sitchin's ancient-astronaut ideas (Sitchin's Anunnaki), is the most prominent proponent of alien and/or far more ancient origins for the site; with Johan Heine he has claimed the sites align with Great Zimbabwe and the Pyramids of Egypt and act as portals to other worlds. These claims are classed as pseudoarchaeology by researchers.

alternatives.label: Other non-local theories
alternatives.text: Earlier, Hromník claimed Indian and "Indo-San" builders (dubbed "the exotic theory" by local researchers), and some proposed the sites were observatories, often linked to non-African construction; these ideas have mostly been rejected.

entries.title: Thonis-Heracleion: the sunken port of Egypt
entries.dateNote: Flourished 6th–4th centuries BCE; fully submerged by the late 8th century CE
entries.mainstream: An Egyptian port near the Canopic mouth of the Nile, now under about 6 m of water in Abu Qir Bay, about 7 km offshore. It was Egypt's main port for international trade in the Late Period (flourishing 6th–4th centuries BCE), with a great temple of Amun-Gereb. It declined as Alexandria rose; around the 2nd century BCE soil liquefaction, floods and earthquakes collapsed the central island, and the last remains sank by the end of the 8th century CE. Located by Franck Goddio's IEASM team with Egypt's antiquities ministry after a five-year search, finds include a Nectanebo I decree stele (found in 2000) proving that "Thonis" and "Heracleion" were one city, statues of Serapis and Arsinoe II, a baris river boat matching Herodotus's description, and a 25 m Ptolemaic galley (announced 2021).

alternatives.label: Legend of Paris and Helen
alternatives.text: Herodotus tells that Paris and Helen of Troy, fleeing Menelaus, landed at the Canopic mouth, where the watchman Thonis seized them; in another version Menelaus and Helen stayed there. Whether such stories preserve any memory is unknown, but the city they named was real.

alternatives.label: Before 2000
alternatives.text: Most historians had thought Thonis and Heracleion were two separate cities on what is now the Egyptian mainland.

entries.changed: Known only from Greek authors until located underwater around 2000; excavations continue (finds announced 2019, 2021, 2023).

entries.title: The "Dendera light"
entries.mainstream: Reliefs in the crypts of the Hathor temple at Dendera, Egypt (temple begun 54 BCE under Ptolemy XII; some crypt reliefs date to his reign). They show the god Harsomtus as a snake emerging from a lotus flower, sometimes inside an oval container (hn), supported by a djed pillar or a kneeling figure. The accompanying hieroglyphic captions identify them as cult statues of Harsomtus, give their sizes (three palms to one cubit) and materials (gold, metal, precious stones), and relate to a creation myth; the crypts were treated as the underworld (Duat), where the gods' statues were kept.

alternatives.label: Ancient electric lamp (speculative)
alternatives.text: A fringe theory holds that the reliefs depict ancient Egyptian electric technology, citing visual similarity to light bulbs, Crookes or Geissler tubes, and the lack of soot in tombs.

alternatives.label: Mainstream reply
alternatives.text: Egyptologists point to the hieroglyphic captions. Bolko Stern showed that copper-topped poles mentioned in temple texts were magical, not electrical, and Kenneth Feder notes that no glass, sockets or filaments have ever been found; soot-free lighting could be explained by mirrors or by adding salt to torches.

entries.title: Modjadji, the Rain Queen
entries.dateNote: Origin traditions set in the 16th century; the queenship continues today
entries.mainstream: The hereditary queen of the Balobedu in Limpopo, South Africa, believed to be able to control clouds and rainfall: bringing rain to allies and drought to enemies. Origin stories trace the line to a chief's daughter, Dzugundini, who fled 16th-century Monomotapa (Zimbabwe) to the Molototsi Valley. By custom the queen avoids public functions, speaks through councillors, presides over an annual November rainmaking ceremony, and does not marry but receives "wives" from subject villages as a diplomatic tie. Eileen and Jack Krige's The Realm of a Rain-Queen (1943) remains a standard study. Her gardens hold the Modjadji cycad, named after her. Masalanabo Modjadji VII took the throne in 2023 after a succession dispute.

alternatives.label: Belief and politics
alternatives.text: Neighbouring communities, and even apartheid-era presidents, historically treated the queen with deference; anthropologists study the rain-making role as a basis of authority and diplomacy.

alternatives.label: Literary echo
alternatives.text: The second Rain Queen, Masalanabo Modjadji, is said to have inspired H. Rider Haggard's novel She, and the title "She-who-must-be-obeyed".

entries.title: Tanganyika laughter epidemic
entries.mainstream: On 30 January 1962 three girls at a mission-run girls' boarding school in Kashasha, on the western shore of Lake Victoria in Tanganyika (now Tanzania), began laughing uncontrollably. It spread to 95 of the 159 pupils; symptoms (laughter and crying, restlessness, pain, fainting, breathing problems, rashes) lasted hours to 16 days. The school closed on 18 March, and a second wave hit when it reopened in May. The episode spread to the village of Nshamba (217 people in April–May), to Ramashenye girls' middle school and to other places within about 100 miles of Bukoba. About 1,000 people were affected and 14 schools shut before it faded after some 18 months. It is generally classed as mass psychogenic illness.

alternatives.label: Stress of independence
alternatives.text: Linguist Christian Hempelmann theorised the outbreak was stress-induced: Tanganyika had just become independent and pupils reported pressure from raised expectations; he notes such illness tends to affect people with little power.

alternatives.label: Cultural dissonance
alternatives.text: Sociologist Robert Bartholomew and psychiatrist Simon Wessely proposed a culture-specific epidemic hysteria arising from conflict between conservative home values and the new ideas of missionary schools.

entries.title: Liangzhu: a Neolithic state drowned by floods?
entries.mainstream: The Liangzhu culture (c. 3300–2300 BCE) of the Yangtze River Delta was the last great Neolithic jade culture of China and is often considered one of East Asia's earliest state societies. Its capital near Hangzhou had 290 hectares within clay walls with six gates, a 30-hectare palace complex (Mojiaoshan), canals, docks, workshops, and dams about 8 km to the north interpreted as an ancient flood-control system. Jade, silk, ivory and lacquer appear only in elite graves. UNESCO inscribed the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City in 2019. After about 2300 BCE the culture vanishes from the Taihu Lake area.

alternatives.label: Floods and rain
alternatives.text: Cultural layers interrupted by muddy, marshy and sandy layers suggest repeated flooding; a 2021 cave-record study (Zhang et al.) found decades of extreme rainfall around 4,345–4,324 years ago, perhaps linked to more frequent El Niño conditions, and concluded that flooding may have forced the abandonment of the capital and the collapse of Liangzhu.

alternatives.label: Part of a wider crisis (interpretation)
alternatives.text: The collapse is sometimes placed in or just before the c. 4.2-kiloyear climate event credited with stressing other early civilisations (Indus, Old Kingdom Egypt, Akkad), though the timing and causes differ by region.

alternatives.label: Pattern note (timeline)
alternatives.text: Chinese tradition places the great flood tamed by Gun and Yu in roughly the same late-third-millennium era (see Gun-Yu flood); no source cited here connects Liangzhu to that story directly.

entries.changed: 1936: first excavated by Shi Xingeng. 2007: city wall base announced. 2019: UNESCO listing. 2021: flood/rainfall collapse study.

sources.title: Collapse of the Liangzhu and other Neolithic cultures in the lower Yangtze region in response to climate change

entries.title: Tarim mummies: "Europeans" in the desert?
entries.dateNote: Earliest c. 2135–1939 BCE; burials continue into the 1st millennium BCE
entries.mainstream: Hundreds of naturally mummified bodies from cemeteries around the Taklamakan Desert in the Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China, many with intact hair (blond, red or brown), woollen textiles and tattoos. The oldest known burials are at Gumugou (c. 2135–1939 BCE), Xiaohe (c. 1884–1736 BCE) and Beifang (c. 1785–1664 BCE); Xiaohe, found by local hunter Ördek in 1911 and excavated by Folke Bergman in 1934, was lost for over 60 years before being relocated by GPS in 2000. Later, Iron Age mummies such as those of the Subeshi culture resemble the Saka (Scythian) Pazyryk culture.

alternatives.label: Western migrants (earlier view)
alternatives.text: Their features and twill and tartan-like textiles (compared by Elizabeth Wayland Barber with Hallstatt finds in Austria) led Mallory and Mair (2000) and others to see "Proto-Europoid" migrants, possibly early speakers of Tocharian Indo-European languages.

alternatives.label: Local isolated population (2021 genomes)
alternatives.text: Zhang et al. (2021) sequenced the oldest mummies and found mostly Ancient North Eurasian ancestry with some Ancient Northeast Asian ancestry and no detectable Western Steppe ancestry: a genetically isolated local population that adopted neighbouring herding and farming practices. Later Tarim groups do show steppe and other ancestries, reflecting several waves of movement.

entries.changed: 1990s–2000s: widely presented as Western/Indo-European migrants. 2003: craniometrics fail to show close European affinity. 2021: ancient genomes point to an isolated local population.
